articles.title: Meta unveils $1,299 VR Glasses, camera-less smart glasses at Meta Connect
articles.summary: Meta debuts its $,1299 VR Glasses.
articles.body:
Meta ( META ) launched three new pairs of smart glasses during the company's Meta Connect conference on Wednesday.

CEO Mark Zuckerberg took the stage to show off the trio of devices, which includes the company's first Meta VR Glasses, the camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses, and the third generation of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

The $1,299 Meta VR Glasses are the standout of the trio, offering virtual reality capabilities in a glasses-style design, which makes other VR headsets look ancient by comparison.

On sale in spring 2027, the company says the high-tech eyewear is five times lighter than its Meta Quest 3 headset, and features a 5K display for watching shows and 3D movies, playing games, and working.

Because you're looking at two screens, there are external cameras so that you can see the world around you while wearing them.

The glass's computing components, battery, and storage are housed in a separate dedicated puck that tethers to the spectacles, helping to ensure they're light enough to wear for long periods.

To navigate, you use hand gestures or can speak to the on-board Muse AI agent. And unlike in the Muse app, you'll see a fully rendered version of your custom Muse avatar.

For film buffs, Meta says the VR Glasses are the first-ever IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device, allowing customers to watch IMAX movies at home.

The company is also partnering with Disney+ ( DIS ) to give users access to movies like "The Avengers" and "Black Panther." Meta says it's working to bring Amazon's ( AMZN ) Prime Video, Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) YouTube, and other streamers to the platform, as well.

In the office, the Meta VR Glasses can display a single large virtual display or several smaller ones, allowing you to switch between apps throughout the day. Flat surfaces turn into virtual keyboards and mice, letting you navigate and type documents without the need for secondary accessories.

For gamers, Microsoft ( MSFT ) is bringing its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to the glasses, so users can play on the go.

Meta is also introducing what it calls its hologram calling technology. Users take a picture of themselves in the Meta AI app, which then creates a full-body digital version of them that they can use to make video calls with friends and family while wearing the glasses. Apple has a similar feature for its Vision Pro headset.

In addition to the Meta VR Glasses, Meta also unveiled the company's $349 Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses.

Unlike the standard Ray-Ban Meta glasses, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses come sans cameras, making them look far more like a standard pair of Ray-Bans.

articles.title: BC reduz para 1,8% estimativa de alta do PIB neste ano e vê nova desaceleração em 2027 | G1
articles.standfirst: Redução no ritmo de crescimento da economia acontece em um cenário de juros ainda altos para tentar conter a inflação. Moderação da atividade neste ano e no próximo tende a criar, também, problemas orçamentários para o governo.
articles.summary: Redução no ritmo de crescimento da economia acontece em um cenário de juros ainda altos para tentar conter a inflação. Moderação da atividade neste ano e no próximo tende a criar, também, problemas orçamentários para o governo.
articles.body:
O Banco Central (BC) reduziu sua estimativa para o crescimento do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) neste ano de 2% para 1,8%. A informação consta no Relatório de Política Monetária do terceiro trimestre, divulgado nesta quinta-feira (24).

Com isso, a autoridade monetária estima desaceleração da economia neste ano, visto que, em 2025, o PIB cresceu 2,3%, conforme divulgação oficial do Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE).

🔎O PIB é a soma de todos os bens e serviços produzidos no país e serve para medir o desempenho da economia. Se o PIB cresce, significa que a economia vai bem e produz mais. Se o PIB cai, quer dizer que a economia está encolhendo. Entretanto, nem sempre crescimento do PIB equivale a bem-estar social.

De acordo com o BC, a queda na estimativa de alta do PIB deste ano incorpora os primeiros indicadores do terceiro trimestre, que sugerem atividade mais fraca do que o previsto anteriormente, e, também, quanto uma "composição menos favorável do crescimento no segundo trimestre".

"Embora o resultado agregado do PIB tenha superado ligeiramente o esperado, as surpresas positivas concentraram-se em segmentos menos sensíveis ao ciclo econômico, notadamente a agropecuária e a indústria extrativa. Os setores mais cíclicos da oferta e o consumo das famílias, por sua vez, surpreenderam em sentido oposto", acrescentou o BC.

➡️Para o ano de 2027, o primeiro de um novo mandato presidencial, o Banco Central estima nova redução no ritmo de crescimento da economia brasileira.

A instituição prevê alta de 1,4% para o Produto Interno Bruto no próximo ano com "expectativa de expansão moderada tanto nos componentes da oferta quanto na demanda".

"A projeção considera a manutenção da política monetária em terreno contracionista [juros altos], a reduzida ociosidade dos fatores de produção, o cenário externo ainda bastante incerto e a diminuição dos impulsos fiscal e creditício. Espera-se, ainda, contribuição mais limitada da agropecuária e da indústria extrativa para o crescimento", informou o BC.

➡️A revisão acontece em um cenário de juros ainda altos para tentar conter a atividade econômic a e, por consequência, a inflação do país — com objetivo de atingir as metas fixadas. Após cinco cortes seguidos, a taxa básica da economia está em 13,75% ao ano. Mesmo assim, é um dos níveis mais altos do planeta em termos reais.

➡️A desaceleração na economia neste ano e no próximo tende a criar, também, problemas orçamentários para o governo devido ao seu efeito de diminuir a arrecadação de impostos e contribuições federais.

➡️No projeto de lei orçamentária de 2027, enviado pelo governo ao Congresso Nacional no fim de agosto, a equipe econômica estimou que o PIB deverá crescer 2,46% no ano que vem.

Esse também é um dos motivos para a Instituição Fiscal Independente (IFI), órgão ligado ao Senado, projetou ter projetado, para o próximo ano, um déficit nas contas do governo da ordem de R$ 86,1 bilhões - enquanto o governo estima saldo positivo de R$ 18,6 bilhões.

"Onde reside a divergência? Primeiro, nos parâmetros macroeconômicos. O PLOA [projeto de lei orçamentária] 2027 ancora-se em uma projeção de expansão do PIB de 2,5%, a IFI projeta um crescimento de 1,8% e o Boletim Focus [mercado financeiro], 1,5%. Isso tem profundas implicações no dimensionamento das receitas públicas: mais ou menos crescimento econômico, mais ou menos recursos disponíveis para financiar a máquina e as políticas públicas", disse o órgão do Senado Federal.

Por conta disso, a IFI avaliou que o governo eleito terá de realizar um bloqueio de gastos no início do próximo ano para tentar atingir a meta de superávit nas suas contas.

articles.title: IBGE quer incluir mercado de drogas ilícitas no PIB; entenda por quê | G1
articles.standfirst: Instituto estuda metodologia que considera número de usuários, consumo médio e preços para estimar o tamanho desse mercado. Primeiros resultados estão previstos para 2028; outros países já adotam cálculo semelhante.
articles.summary: Instituto estuda metodologia que considera número de usuários, consumo médio e preços para estimar o tamanho desse mercado. Primeiros resultados estão previstos para 2028.
articles.body:
O Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística (IBGE) prepara a inclusão de uma estimativa sobre a comercialização de drogas ilícitas no cálculo do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) do país.

A mudança está sendo desenvolvida como parte da revisão periódica do Sistema de Contas Nacionais (SCN), e os primeiros resultados da nova metodologia estão previstos para ser divulgados em 2028.

A mudança não significa que o IBGE passará a considerar o tráfico de drogas uma atividade legal ou que passará a medir crimes em geral. O objetivo é estimar uma atividade econômica que efetivamente movimenta dinheiro e, dessa forma, evitar que parte da produção, da renda e dos gastos realizados no país fique fora das estatísticas econômicas.

🔎 O Reino Unido, por exemplo, passou a incluir estimativas sobre drogas ilícitas em suas Contas Nacionais em 2014. França, Alemanha, Suécia, Holanda, Itália, Espanha e Hungria estão entre os países que também adotam a metodologia europeia.

Por que uma atividade ilegal entra no cálculo do PIB?

O instituto começou a discutir como estimar esse mercado em 2019 e realizou uma primeira estimativa-teste em 2021. Desde então, os estudos e os testes metodológicos continuam. A inclusão fará parte da próxima revisão estrutural das Contas Nacionais, processo que o IBGE realiza aproximadamente a cada 10 anos.

O PIB mede o valor dos bens e serviços produzidos em uma economia em determinado período. Nas Contas Nacionais, o critério não é simplesmente saber se uma atividade é permitida ou proibida pela legislação.

As regras internacionais preveem que, quando há uma transação econômica voluntária entre comprador e vendedor, ela pode entrar nas contas mesmo que o bem ou serviço comercializado seja ilegal.

É o caso da compra e venda de drogas: embora a produção e o comércio sejam proibidos, existe uma transação de mercado entre quem vende e quem compra.

Segundo os manuais internacionais consultados pelo IBGE, como o System of National Accounts (SNA), publicado pela ONU, e o "Handbook on the compilation of statistics on illegal economic activities in national accounts and balance of payments", deixar essas operações completamente fora das contas pode produzir distorções em outras partes das estatísticas.

Um exemplo é o cálculo da poupança das famílias. Se uma família gasta dinheiro na compra de um produto ilegal e esse gasto não é registrado, as contas podem dar a impressão de que aquele dinheiro permaneceu com a família. Na prática, ele foi gasto.

O resultado é uma possível superestimativa da poupança e uma inconsistência entre as diferentes contas econômicas.

🔎 No caso do Brasil, o IBGE informou em nota que incluirá a comercialização de drogas ilícitas no cálculo do PIB. Entretanto, os materiais internacionais nos quais o instituto se baseia tratam de três tipos de atividades ilícitas: drogas, prostituição e contrabando. Questionado, o IBGE não explicou se levará em consideração somente as drogas ou também as outras duas atividades.

Como o IBGE pretende calcular o tamanho desse mercado?

O cálculo não parte simplesmente da quantidade de drogas apreendida pela polícia. A metodologia internacional recomenda começar principalmente pelo lado da demanda, ou seja, tentar estimar quanto é consumido.

Isso acontece porque é muito difícil observar diretamente a produção e a venda em um mercado ilegal. Produtores e traficantes têm incentivo para esconder suas atividades. Já as informações sobre consumo podem ser obtidas por meio de pesquisas e de outras estatísticas disponíveis.

De forma simplificada, a estimativa parte de três elementos:

Número de usuários × consumo médio por usuário × preço de venda = estimativa do gasto dos consumidores.

A partir daí, o cálculo precisa estimar como esse consumo é abastecido: quanto vem da produção nacional e quanto corresponde a drogas que entram no território brasileiro por meio de importações ilegais.

Também é necessário estimar os custos envolvidos na atividade. Isso permite chegar ao chamado Valor Adicionado Bruto (VAB), que mede quanto uma atividade efetivamente acrescenta à economia depois de descontados os bens e serviços utilizados na produção.

articles.title: Gold Holds Drop as Higher Oil and Hot US Data Fan Rate-Hike Bets
articles.summary: Gold held a decline as resurgent energy prices and stronger-than-expected US economic data increased bets the Federal Reserve might again raise interest rate...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Gold held a decline as resurgent energy prices and stronger-than-expected US economic data increased bets the Federal Reserve might again raise interest rates to combat inflation.

Bullion was trading around $4,290 an ounce, after falling 1.7% the day before. Oil rose after a defiant Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the United Nations his country won't allow freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz while sanctions and a US blockade remain in place, underscoring the difficulty in reaching a peace deal with Washington despite efforts to revive talks this week.

He added that Iran is ready to negotiate but will not respond to threats, and while it isn't interested in building an atomic weapon, it won't give up the right to develop nuclear technology for economic reasons. This comes a day after President Donald Trump said his officials had "very good" talks with Iranian envoys on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Gold has been dictated by the Fed's rate outlook in recent weeks as investors gauge whether surging energy prices will keep inflationary pressure strong enough to prompt further increases in rates, which would likely be negative for bullion as it pays no interest. It's down around a fifth since the US-Iran war erupted in late February.

Losses in the US Treasuries market intensified on stronger-than-forecast economic data and a weak debt auction, reflecting the view that inflation is likely to remain sticky. Treasury yields across most maturities hit the highest in almost two decades, while five-year US yields moved above 5% for the first time since 2007.

US business activity rose at the fastest pace in more than five years as robust demand pushed up new orders and employment at manufacturers and service providers. The S&P Global flash US composite purchasing managers index climbed to 58.4 in September, the highest since July 2021.

Fed Governor Michael Barr said further rate increases are likely needed to return inflation to the central bank's 2% target. His comments follow a string of similar warnings from fellow policymakers in recent days that price pressures appear to be persistent. Swap markets are currently pricing in at least three hikes by April next year, an increase from earlier this week.

articles.body: NSE IPO listing date today: National Stock Exchange of India’s shares debuted on the Bombay Stock Exchange at Rs 1,800 versus an issue price of Rs 1,785, marking a premium of around 0.8%.NSE made its stock market debut with a market capitalisation of more than Rs 4.45 lakh crore, becoming the second listed stock exchange in India. Its valuation at listing was significantly higher than that of rival BSE, whose current market capitalisation stands at Rs 1.33 lakh crore.Market participants were tracking grey market movements closely ahead of the listing, which is among the most anticipated market debuts of the year so far. Analysts said restrictions on exits by most large shareholders could limit the availability of NSE shares in the near term, potentially putting upward pressure on prices at a later stage.NSE's market debut gives investors an opportunity to assess how the exchange should be valued. Its longer-term growth outlook helped attract strong institutional interest, while retail investors appeared more cautious amid concerns about derivatives volumes, regulatory pressures and the possibility of more shares entering the market.Although investors remain broadly positive on NSE's longer-term prospects, the stock's performance in the months following its listing could depend on the amount of additional equity that becomes available once the lock-in periods for existing shareholders come to an end.NSE Debuts on BSE, MSEIIn a circular issued on Wednesday, MSE said NSE's equity shares would be admitted for trading on its capital market segment under the ‘Permitted to trade’ category, effective September 24.The Metropolitan Stock Exchange is a Sebi-recognised national stock exchange that operates an electronic trading platform covering capital markets, equity derivatives, currency derivatives and debt segments. Its platform includes equity and index derivatives, debt and currency derivatives, with more than 250 listings and over 3,100 companies available for trading.The development comes days after NSE MD and CEO Ashish Chauhan made it clear that the exchange would not approach Sebi for permission to trade its own shares on its platform. Existing regulations of the market regulator do not permit a recognised stock exchange to list its own securities on its own trading platform.NSE IPO GMPIn the unlisted market, traders saw a grey market premium or GMP of around 2.2%. The stock has listed on a waek note with less than 1% premium over its issue price.The GMP was much higher earlier at Rs 250-310 a share, or roughly 14-17%. The steep decline had suggested expectations of only modest gains when the shares list."While investors have been waiting for the NSE listing for long, the enthusiasm has moderated because of the large issue size and expected supply," Abhay Doshi, co-founder of UnlistedArena.com told ET.At the IPO's upper price of Rs 1,785 per share, NSE's valuation stands at Rs 4.42 lakh crore, compared with Rs 1.33 lakh crore for rival BSE. Some market participants said the balance between available supply and investor demand could play an important role in determining how NSE shares perform in the initial trading sessions after listing.The listing brings to an end NSE's long-running journey towards becoming a listed company and make it India's second listed stock exchange after BSE.NSE launched its initial public offering earlier this month, seeking to raise Rs 22,562 crore through a 12.64 crore-share offer for sale (OFS) by existing shareholders.Since the issue was entirely an OFS, NSE itself will not receive any money from the IPO. The proceeds will instead accrue to the shareholders selling their stakes through the offering.The IPO price band was fixed at Rs 1,700 to Rs 1,785 per share. With the lot size set at 8 shares, retail investors were required to invest a minimum of Rs 14,280 to apply for the issue.Before the IPO opened for subscription, NSE had raised Rs 6,746 crore from more than 150 anchor investors.Foreign portfolio investors made up Rs 2,883 crore, or 43%, of the total anchor book. The anchor round saw participation from more than 20 foreign long-only funds, including Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Norges Bank.Domestic institutional participation was similarly spread across investors. More than 25 mutual funds, along with 11 insurance and pension companies, invested around Rs 3,588 crore, accounting for 53% of the anchor book.LIC, which is NSE's largest shareholder with a 10.72% stake, also participated in the anchor round. LIC, LIC Mutual Fund and LIC Pension Fund together invested more than Rs 500 crore. The investment was made even though LIC's existing shareholding in NSE is larger than the stake being offered through the IPO.The SBI group also took part in the anchor book through SBI Mutual Fund, SBI General, SBI Life and SBI Pension Fund. State Bank of India and SBI Capital Markets are together selling a 1% stake in NSE, while the group's combined investment in the exchange through its various entities exceeds Rs 400 crore.NSE's first public issue attracted strong demand during the three-day subscription period from September 17 to September 21. The IPO was subscribed nearly six times the shares on offer. Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) drove the demand, subscribing to their reserved portion around 13 times, while the portions allocated to retail investors and non-institutional investors (NII) were subscribed 1.4 times and 6.6 times, respectively.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tokyo Used Condo Prices Drop for First Time in Over Two Years
articles.summary: Used condominium prices in Tokyo dropped for the first time in more than two years in August as rising mortgage rates start to weigh on sentiment among home...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Used condominium prices in Tokyo dropped for the first time in more than two years in August as rising mortgage rates start to weigh on sentiment among home buyers, according to a research firm.

The average price of condos in Japan's capital dropped 0.2% from the previous month to ¥112.74 million ($714,000), marking the first decline in 28 months, Tokyo Kantei Co. wrote in a report released Thursday. Prices began falling in previous months in the more expensive city center areas, suggesting that weakness in the city's condominium market is spreading.

Mortgage costs are climbing in Japan as the central bank raises interest rates and signals its willingness to tighten credit further, damping condo demand from home buyers. Japan's Financial Services Agency has said it will strengthen its oversight of real estate lending amid concern that property prices are overshooting in Tokyo, driven by domestic and international investors rushing in, chasing capital gains.

"Price adjustments for properties in central Tokyo are expected to continue toward the end of the year," said Masayuki Takahashi, senior principal researcher at Tokyo Kantei. "Similar movements will continue not only in central Tokyo but also in surrounding areas."

Highlighting the earlier condo price declines in the more expensive areas of the metropolis, the average price of properties in Tokyo's six central wards fell 0.7% from the previous month, marking the fourth consecutive month of declines. The prices are adjusted to represent 70 square meter units.

articles.title: Trump and Xi summit will focus on ‘stabilising’ ties, experts say
articles.summary: Trade, AI and security are on the agenda, but experts say rebuilding trust may take priority over major deals.
articles.body:
As United States President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping with a rare personal welcome at the airport, to be followed by a state banquet and a military flyover, experts warn to temper expectations as the summit is more focused on “re-establishing trust” rather than having any meaningful deals announced at the end of it.

The US and China have been locked in a trade war since Trump’s first term as president when he introduced levies on imports of certain industrial goods, and Beijing retaliated with tariffs on a range of US exports including soya beans, pork and electric vehicles. Some of those policies continued under Trump’s successor, President Joe Biden, who also introduced other measures, including curbs on chip exports.

But relations really nosedived with Trump’s second term when he unleashed new tariffs on China, including threatening levies of 200 percent at one point last year, with Beijing promising to hit back at similar levels and throttling exports of critical minerals that are used in manufacturing a range of products from laptops and cellphones to cars and renewable energy infrastructure.

While both sides have since stepped back from that cliff after the two leaders met in late October in Busan on the sidelines of the APEC summit in South Korea, US tariffs are still at a hefty average of 36.5 percent, while China’s tariffs on US goods average out to 31 percent.

“This is not a bargaining summit,” Reza Hasmath, academic faculty adviser at The China Institute at the University of Alberta, told Al Jazeera. “It’s a stabilising summit.”

Apart from tariffs, other items on the agenda include cooperation on artificial intelligence safety, Iran and Taiwan.

“The point of the summit is to set up a continuation of the truce” that was arrived at in Busan, said Mary E Lovely, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute of International Economics.

It was after that meeting that China resumed its supply of critical minerals. The US wants those deliveries to be sped up and “for that reason alone, the US will want a continuation of the truce”, Lovely added.

With that goal, Lovely says there may be an announcement of a Board of Trade mechanism where both sides would reduce their respective tariffs on $30bn worth of goods each.

For Lovely, the best-case scenario from the summit will be the two countries actually do begin to liberalise trade of some non-sensitive goods and that the flow of critical minerals is indeed sped up, all of which will show “a little bit of normalisation of relations”. The worst case, on the other hand, is if they don’t find common ground, she said.

Safety rules around AI and a coordinated slowdown in that sector, for instance, could be tricky topics, experts agree.

While US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has proposed a US-China dialogue and an AI hotline to report AI incidents that could threaten national security, the lack of mutual trust will limit any real deliverables in this area, says Dexter Tiff Roberts, nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Global China Hub.

The distrust is fuelled by US restrictions on the sale of advanced chips to China, as well as repeated rhetoric from the US government, including from Trump, that there is a battle for supremacy in AI that the US must win.

At the same time, “China wants to push global governance on its own terms and sees AI as a soft power tool that they can offer to other countries”, said Tiff Roberts.

Similarly, on Iran, while China does not sell weapons to Tehran, it does sell dual-use components. It also has historically bought significant quantities of oil from Iran, revenues from which have helped the latter’s economy stay afloat.

Although it has held off those purchases in the past few months of the US-Iran war – thus helping stabilise global oil prices – as it has dipped into its strategic reserves, experts say that could change in the near future.

Beijing “is delighted that the US is distracted with its war in Iran”, said Tiff Roberts, “and is not going to do anything to help the US with that”.

Taiwan is democratically governed, but China views it as its own territory and wants to see the US moving closer to its policy. Taiwan, which rejects unification, has been waiting for months for Washington, DC, to approve the sale of $14bn in arms .

“We don’t expect Trump to sell Taiwan down the river … but Trump is a bit of a wild card, and Taiwan is nervously watching,” said Tiff Roberts.

Even though no real deals are expected from the three-day summit, experts agree that it is important for the two leaders to meet.

“There’s a whole lot at stake given the huge trade relationship, including for the rest of the world,” Tiff Roberts said.

Also, as Trump heads into the US midterm elections, he “wants a big state visit to show he’s an international leader of standing and wants the bright lights of TV on him to show him as a leader”, while China needs a better trade relationship, especially as its domestic economy sags, said Tiff Roberts.

But at the end of the day, “it will be a horse and pony show, with a few not very meaningful announcements. But it will be about re-establishing trust”, said the China Institute’s Hasmath.

articles.body: Stock market crash today: Nifty50 and BSE Sensex, the Indian equity benchmark indices ended sharply lower on Thursday, weighed down by weak global cues and a steep rise in US bond yields.The Nifty 50 closed at 23,063.10, down 383.70 points, or 1.64%, while the BSE Sensex settled at 73,580.54, lower by 1,247.71 points, or 1.67%.The market came under heavy selling pressure during the session, with both indices falling above 1.5% as US bond yields climbed to a 19-year high, adding to concerns among investors.Bajaj Finance emerged as the biggest drag on the Sensex, with its shares plunging more than 5%. Axis Bank and Bajaj Finserv also came under significant pressure, declining 3-4%. Shares of IndiGo, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Asian Paints, HDFC Bank and Trent were lower by 1-2%.The selloff was not limited to large-cap stocks. The Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 indices each fell around 1%, reflecting weakness across the broader market, according to an ET report. Every sectoral index was trading in negative territory, with the Nifty Private Bank and Nifty Financial Services indices losing around 2% each.Why did stock market fall today?Bond yields climbUS Treasury yields jumped sharply after data indicated that business activity in the US accelerated to its strongest level in more than five years in September. The rise in yields added to pressure on equities.The interest rate-sensitive 2-year US Treasury yield briefly moved above 4.9%, marking its highest level since May 2024. Meanwhile, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose 13.89 basis points to 5.106%, its highest level since 2007 and its steepest single-day increase since April 2025.A sharp increase in bond yields can make debt-market investments more appealing to investors. This can, in turn, put pressure on equities as some investors shift towards fixed-income assets.Fed rate hike expectationsThe pressure on equities intensified as market expectations for a sharp increase in US interest rates strengthened. Traders in Fed funds futures are now assigning a 66% probability to a rate hike in October, compared with 53% earlier in the day. The shift came after data showed US business activity had climbed to its highest level in more than five years in September.Oil prices riseConcerns were further heightened by a renewed increase in oil prices, with crude moving back above $102 per barrel after slipping below $99 on Wednesday. The rise came amid continued differences between Iran and the US over efforts to end the war.Rupee fallsThe rupee also came under pressure in early trading, declining 14 paise to 95.87 against the US dollar. The fall came as oil prices and bond yields rose sharply.“The rupee continues to hover in the 95.60-95.95 zone, with persistent FII selling in Indian markets keeping sentiment cautious. Going ahead, US-Iran developments, Xi Jinping’s US visit and UN meeting updates could keep currency markets volatile,” said Jateen Trivedi, VP Research Analyst - Commodity and Currency, LKP Securities.Insurance stocks tankShares of insurance distributor PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar, took a severe hit after Irdai proposed changes to the insurance sector, with the stock plunging as much as 30% and the company losing more than Rs 26,200 crore in market value.PB Fintech shares fell through multiple circuit limits on the NSE, dropping 30% to Rs 1,320.10 apiece. articles.title: McDonald’s is spending billions to make major changes
articles.summary: McDonald’s is spending billions of dollars to boost its franchises, an effort to cement its title as the leader in fast food amid growing competition.
articles.body: McDonald’s is spending billions of dollars to boost its franchises, an effort to cement its title as the leader in fast food amid growing competition. The chain announced Wednesday that it will invest $8.5 billion by 2036 on a series of initiatives, including remodeling restaurants, retraining their 2 million employees and adding new menu items to target high-protein eaters. About $5 billion will be spent in the next three-and-a-half years alone, a combination of capital support as well as rent relief for franchises. It’s all part of multiyear strategy to win back diners and capture more market share. Last month, McDonald’s reported its slowest quarterly growth since 2025. The chain had blamed the decline on launching too many promotions, inadequate customer service and its massive World Cup promotion failing to attract eaters. The new strategy, called “Next,” aims to make the chain “the first choice for more customers, more often — while making our restaurants stronger and easier to run,” CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a press release. McDonald’s troubles are part of broader economic issues affecting all dining chains, like rising food prices causing customers to dine out less. The chain’s stock have fallen about 20% for the year. What’s new? In addition to rent relief and capital support, some of that multibillion-dollar spend will be used for remodeling restaurants. McDonald’s mandates its franchises remodel every decade. Images revealed on Wednesday show expansive dining rooms, bigger play areas and improved lighting. There are also redesigned kitchens that will use new AI tools to improve speed and efficiency, which the company said it expects to earn each restaurant an additional $100,000 in cash flow via savings. McDonald’s also focused on changing its menu as it combats new competition, such as: a revitalized Burger King, beverages from fast-growing upstarts, and chicken-centric chains rolling out nuggets and tenders. Notably, Burger King posted an 8.5% increase in US same-store sales last quarter, outpacing McDonald’s by the largest margin in more than a decade. McDonald’s also noted a growing market of protein seekers, which it said amounts to 60 million Americans as well as 30 million GLP-1 users. The chain is testing burger and chicken bowls, egg bites and more grilled chicken options, like in wraps. Customers “want more protein, greater portion flexibility and food that leaves them feeling satisfied without feeling like too much,” McDonald’s USA president Skye Anderson said at the company’s investor day on Wednesday. A new value menu is also also being discussed with its franchisees that will replace its recently introduced “$3 and Under” menu, Kempczinski said. Last month, he said restaurants “were overwhelmed by too many deployments (of promotions) in the quarter, which led to less efficient restaurant operations… and impacted customer service times.” In addition to previously announced drinks, the chain is focusing on installing new espresso machines and offering alternative milks in an attempt to improve coffee sales. Lastly, McDonald’s is launching a new program on October 5 to retrain its 2 million employees worldwide. Rivals, like Burger King and Starbucks, are rolling out similar programs as customers grow tired of self-service technology. “While there is so much our customers love, we are falling short when it comes to consistent execution,” Anderson said Wednesday.

articles.title: Not everyone thinks AI will kill us all
articles.summary: When AI company Hugging Face was hacked by a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents who had escaped their testing environment, the company’s CEO had many things to say.
articles.body: When AI company Hugging Face was hacked by a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents who had escaped their testing environment, the company’s CEO had many things to say. He called it an unprecedented event – “day one for cybersecurity in the age of agents.” But here’s one thing he didn’t say: The hack is a sign AI is going to be able to eventually wipe out humanity. Clement Delangue doesn’t buy into the doomer hype that’s gone viral in recent weeks, even as the victim of likely the most sophisticated AI agent-powered attack (that we know of). He scoffed at former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, when he posted on X that the people building AI are “gambling with our lives” because they believe it “will kill us all.” “Asking (Coxon) about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change,” Delangue posted on X. “Not saying it’s necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let’s keep things in perspective and hear from the full range of expertise across the ecosystem!” It’s easy to get the impression that everyone in AI is worried about it causing human extinction. But that’s not the case. There are plenty of scientists, industry researchers, and executives who believe the risks are overblown, and the technology is the way toward a new golden age. AI’s biggest backer isn’t scared Yes, there are major safety concerns surrounding AI, these anti-doomer AI scientists and other industry veterans say. But they maintain that AI is not going to wipe out humanity in the next few years, as some have predicted. Each has their own reasoning – some say any action AI would take that could wipe out humanity would need heavy involvement from human accomplices. Then there’s those who say AI at the end of the day is a computer program that can be engineered, and others who say that engineers are getting better and better at keeping AI from going rogue. Still others worry that by raising alarms about a hypothetical extinction risk, some may be seeking to direct policymaking in a way that could benefit some companies over others. One of the loudest voices has been Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company not only dominates the AI chips industry, but also has stakes in many other major AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. He told CBS News on Sunday that there is a “0% chance” AI will cause the end of humanity by 2030. “Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible,” Huang added. Huang has pushed back against the so-called “doomers” for years. He did not sign a 2023 Center for AI Safety one-sentence statement that stated: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from A.I. should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks, such as pandemics and nuclear war.” (The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind all signed the statement). In 2023, he told the New Yorker he has never worried about AI technology. His comments have only grown more forceful since then. In July, he told Axios that the idea that AI is going to be the end of humanity as “complete nonsense.” Huang also rejected calls from other AI leaders for greater AI regulation, saying it’s up to the companies to pace themselves. Recent incidents of AI agents going rogue, taking unsanctioned actions and hacking into other companies is just an issue of a product not being ready to be released, he said. “That’s engineering, good old-fashioned engineering,” he told reporters at an AI summit hosted by Britain’s King Charles III last week. “This is no different than, you know, an omelet’s not ready to be released, or a car is not ready to be released, an airplane engine’s not ready to be released. You should properly test it.” Then there’s Turing Award-winning computer scientist Yann LeCun, considered by many in the industry to be one of the “godfathers of AI” and the former chief AI scientist at Meta. LeCun responded bluntly to a user who claimed AI “will get us all killed in three years”: “No, Not a chance in hell,” he said. “AI folks who live in the discrete world of bits and tokens don’t always understand how incredibly messy the real world is,” he added. LeCun has compared the panicked responses to recent AI incidents to blaming the entire plumbing industry for one bad plumber’s mistake, LeCun said. Risks, but not existential ones Not everyone dismisses the risk quite so bluntly, though. Aidan Gomez, CEO of Cohere, a leader in the open-weight AI model space, told CNN in a recent interview that the “doomer” talk is “misleading and scary.” Gomez lamented that the public may be getting “this skewed perspective” that the entire industry says AI poses an immediate existential risk to humans, “which is fundamentally not true,” he said. Where Huang and LeCun wave the extinction scenario away almost entirely, Gomez draws a more specific line: He says there are real risks, just not the ones getting the most attention right now. The “most significant national security threat” posed by AI is cyberattacks, Gomez said, especially if such powerful tools fall into the wrong hands, or are being utilized by nation states for offensive operations. Today, “you just need a data center, and overnight you have like a country’s population of the world’s best hackers at your disposal.” As for misalignment — the fear that AI agents could go rogue on their own — Gomez said that’s “a concern,” but one he considers far more manageable than the cyber threat. He said the industry is “getting quite good at measuring it, getting quite good at detecting it.” Rumman Chowdhury, US science envoy for AI under former President Joe Biden, takes the skepticism a step further, questioning not just the odds of an AI-driven extinction event but the mechanics of how one would even happen. While AI could be used to help kill humans, she argues, it would need human involvement to set it off. “And then what? It uses the machines to actually make a physical virus, and then it, what, calls FedEx?” Chowdhury, now CEO of the safety firm Human Intelligence PBC, told CNN in an interview, referring to the often-referenced warning of AI creating a killer virus. “Like, what is this mechanism?” Chowdhury said she believes that researchers like Coxon are being honest that they think AI poses an existential risk. “But are his beliefs reality? No, his beliefs are not,” she said. For Chowdhury, the sincerity of that belief is almost beside the point. What worries her is that such existential fears could distract from present harms the technology is already causing, such as AI deepfakes, mental health challenges and the potential for job loss. Then there’s the loudest voice dismissing these concerns, which is also one of the most powerful: President Donald Trump, who has thus far defied calls for the US government to get more involved in setting standards or regulating the industry and called the recent alarm over AI “a hoax.” “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote earlier this month.

articles.title: Why the runaway 10-year yield is triggering this bad memory for investors
articles.summary: An ominous sign on bonds.
articles.body:
The fresh rip in the 10-year US Treasury yield is triggering a brutal memory in the minds of many investors.

They aren't necessarily admitting it, as seen in the stock market's surprising resilience.

The last time the US 10-year bond yield was this high was July 2007. Three months later, the global financial crisis started as the housing meltdown shocked the world. The Nasdaq Composite plunged 56% over the next 16 months, points out the team at Bull Theory.

Now we aren't currently living in a global financial meltdown by any means. And to suggest we are on the cusp of a stock market crash simply because yields are back to 2007 levels would be reckless.

But it does bear watching, and it does bear perhaps reigning in one's risk appetite for stocks.

The 10-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.12% on Wednesday, its highest level since 2007. The 30-year Treasury yield touched 5.37% while the 5-year yield also jumped to a 2007 high.

The move higher in yields comes as oil prices advanced and business activity data came in hotter than expected. Taken together, it fueled concerns about further Fed rate hikes.

New York Federal Reserve president John Williams said Thursday it was reasonable to think the Fed may need to raise interest rates again before year-end to corral inflation.

Williams echoed Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr's comments on Wednesday that additional interest rate hikes would be needed.

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team. Follow Sozzi on X @BrianSozzi , Instagram , and LinkedIn . Tips on stories? Email brian.sozzi@yahoofinance.com.

articles.title: Why so many Americans leave Social Security money on the table
articles.summary: Many pre-retirees plan to start Social Security before full retirement age and accept lower lifetime benefits.
articles.body:
More than half of working Americans worry about outliving their money in retirement, yet many of those same people plan to begin collecting Social Security benefits early — leaving money on the table.

If you delay benefits from your full retirement age (for most people, that's 67) until age 70, you earn delayed retirement credits — about an 8% increase each year until you hit 70.

But more than a quarter of Social Security beneficiaries begin claiming benefits at age 62, as soon as they're eligible, even though their monthly benefit may be slashed by as much as 30%.

Just 10% expect to hold off until age 70.

"There is no single right age for claiming Social Security," said Deb Boyden, head of US defined contribution at Schroders, which recently published its retirement survey for 2026. "What stands out, though, is how remarkably consistent this behavior has been."

In 2024, 43% of nonretired Americans said they planned to begin claiming Social Security before age 67. That increased to 44% in 2025, Boyden said.

For now, Social Security pays, on average, about $25,000 a year in retirement benefits — scarcely enough to get by comfortably.

The size of your Social Security check depends on your work history, lifetime earnings, retirement age, and the year you start claiming benefits.

Most Americans don't wait or simply can't delay until age 70 to start collecting benefits, but if you can, you wind up with more cash in your bank account.

People know that. They've done the math, according to the new findings.

So what's driving these self-defeating choices? Financial need, more than likely.

"It suggests that financial necessity and financial confidence may matter more than knowledge alone," Boyden said.

Americans are willing to forgo that extra monthly income, despite their angst about running short in retirement. "Their reasons are practical," she added.

They include things like expecting to need the money sooner to live on, wanting access to it as soon as possible, or concerns that Social Security may run out of money or stop making payments.

To Boyden, that suggests many Americans are making personal decisions "based on current financial realities" rather than thinking about maximizing their Social Security checks in the future.

The main reason people start their Social Security checks before they get to age 70 is "first and foremost their income needs," said Jacob Cornell, a financial adviser based in Sarasota, Fla.

Roughly one-quarter of American workers have access to employer-provided paid family leave benefits,…
articles.body:
Many working families struggle to balance work and caregiving responsibilities, but a bipartisan majority on Capitol Hill are unveiling legislation seeking to make life easier for American families when it comes to paid leave, family tax credits and federal child savings accounts.

Roughly one-quarter of American workers have access to employer-provided paid family leave benefits, but disparities among state paid leave policies create compliance challenges for employers operating in multiple states.

During this timely program, we will discuss expanding access to paid leave through an innovative state-driven, public-private partnership model while creating a national framework that allows employers to administer these benefits efficiently across state lines.

We will also explore family tax credits and federal child savings accounts — two areas where lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are advancing proposals to ease costs for new families and build long-term savings for children.

Join The Hill, in partnership with American Policy Ventures Foundation, for a “Future of Supporting American Families” bipartisan summit — where we will do a deep dive into policies assisting American workers and families with lawmakers, policymakers and pollsters.

The event is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. ET.

articles.title: Trump trade rules apply differently to China, Canada, and Xi, Carney
articles.summary: President Trump heads into his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week on the heels of waging a bruising trade war with Canada that has badly damaged relations with that country. It’s a stark contrast from how he’s handled trade talks with China, a rival nation that many in Congress see as an enemy…
articles.body:
President Trump heads into his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week on the heels of waging a bruising trade war with Canada that has badly damaged relations with that country.

It’s a stark contrast from how he’s handled trade talks with China, a rival nation that many in Congress see as an enemy of the United States, but that is the world’s second-largest economy .

While Canada has long been a U.S. ally, Trump has a frosty relationship with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. With China, Trump has long touted his relationship with Xi, which he has described as strong.

The different approaches make sense in the context of Trump. He sees China as offering more to the U.S., and he wants Beijing’s cooperation on a host of other issues, from Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war .

But it is also an example of Trump’s great-powers approach to economic and foreign policy.

“The administration’s approach to China and Canada has diverged sharply, and leverage helps explain why,” Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, told The Hill on Wednesday.

“China holds cards Washington cannot easily replace, particularly in rare earth processing, agricultural demand and global manufacturing,” Krishnan added. “That constrains how far the White House can push and has produced a more calibrated, transactional approach to Beijing.”

Multiple Republican lawmakers, including Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), have raised concerns about the president’s trade war with Canada.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) did not mention the U.S.-Canada tariff dispute on Tuesday during remarks on the Senate floor. Instead, the Senate Armed Services Committee chair blasted Xi ahead of his visit to Washington.

“Quite frankly, had the White House asked me for advice, I would have suggested the president not invite Xi Jinping to Washington for such a lavish welcome here in the United States of America,” Wicker remarked .

The summit comes less than two months before a Nov. 10 deadline for the U.S. and China to extend a trade truce the sides reached last year.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly defended Xi’s visit in a statement to The Hill.

“President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week. The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people,” Kelly said.

Ahead of Xi’s arrival in the states, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday in New York City. A day after that gathering, Greer acknowledged that while the two sides made “headway,” officials needed more time to hash out an extension of the truce.

“My expectation is we’ll continue talking, and I think both sides want it,” Greer told host Annmarie Hordern on “Bloomberg Surveillance.”

When Hordern later asked the trade representative about a three- to six-month extension, he said that was “probably the right” range.

Bessent also offered a peek behind the curtain at his and Greer’s meeting with He, saying Monday the impending deadline was a “focal point” of discussions.

“In Beijing, this notion of a, what we call a 30 by 30 trade deal for noncritical goods was floated,” Bessent told host Joe Kernen on CNBC’s “Squawk Box,” referencing Trump and Xi’s last summit in May.

Under such a deal, the U.S. and China would reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of noncritical goods each country imports from the other, Bessent noted.

That would mean U.S. businesses would export more agricultural goods, energy-related products and medical devices to China, while Beijing would purchase more “everyday items” from America, the Treasury secretary remarked.

Bessent also met with He on Wednesday in Washington, D.C., and wrote on the social platform X their discussions centered on “securing meaningful commitments that protect American workers, farmers, and businesses.”

How the president and his officials have approached trade talks with China differs greatly from their attitude toward Carney and Canada amid a North American trade war .

After Carney called out trade discussions last month, Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods went into effect — applying to roughly 7 percent of the $382 billion U.S. businesses imported from Canada last year.

Carney responded in kind, matching American tariffs “dollar for dollar” earlier this month. Trump then doubled down, signing executive orders to ban the sale of Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages starting Sept. 29.

Trump has spent his second term mocking Canada and expressing interest in annexing the country. The president also called America’s northern neighbor a “terrible trade partner” last week.

The Canadian prime minister, meanwhile, has used the trade war to shift his focus to strengthening relationships with other Western nations.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed that Canada join the European Union as an associate member, while Carney argued earlier this month the era of Canadian “dependence” on America was over .

“For the past year and a half, we’ve been steering our economy towards trusted partners,” Carney said in a video message his office released on the day the retaliatory tariffs went into effect.

The Trump-Carney tensions contrast with how the president has characterized his relationship with Xi dating back to his first term.

While he has slapped tariffs on Chinese imports as far back as 2018, Trump has sought to forge closer ties with Xi on the likes of critical minerals and the Iran war — despite Beijing’s longtime economic and military alliance with the Islamic Republic.

Bessent highlighted Trump and Xi’s “very good relationship” on Monday, saying on CNBC the two leaders “have great respect for each other.”

Wicker said Tuesday that Trump will “rightfully” discuss trade and artificial intelligence with Xi, noting the possibility for the two leaders to make “progress” on those issues.

But the Mississippi Republican urged the president to “keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator,” during the summit, which kicked off Wednesday with Trump greeting Xi at Joint Base Andrews.

Trump’s decision to meet Xi at the base also underscores his differing approaches to world leaders.

Julian Gewirtz, who worked in the State Department during former President Biden’s administration, said Trump’s embrace of Xi is part of a “pattern,” in which the president “views Xi Jinping, [Russian President] Vladimir Putin, these autocratic leaders of large states as his peers, as leaders who merit this degree” of respect.

“Whereas, of course, the leaders of traditional U.S. allies do not get this kind of treatment,” Gewirtz said on Wednesday’s episode of “The President’s Inbox” podcast, adding he does not think “we’re ever going to live to see the day when President Trump greets Mark Carney on a tarmac.”

The second of four meetings in 2026 between the leaders of the United States and China is unlikely to produce any major breakthroughs.

Despite Trump’s courting of Xi, analysts are not certain the two sides will extend the trade truce. Krishnan put the odds of a predeadline extension around 70 percent, arguing neither side “has much to gain from returning” to prior tariff rates.

“An extension would preserve a period of relative stability rather than resolve the underlying contest,” she wrote.

articles.title: Tesla Semi event puts the spotlight on trucking as busy month for EV maker rolls on
articles.summary: Tesla will open the doors to its new Semi factory in Sparks, Nevada on Thursday, just as investors look for proof that the long-delayed electric Semi is fina...
articles.body:
Tesla ( TSLA ) will open the doors to its new Semi factory in Sparks, Nevada, on Thursday, just as investors look for proof that the long-delayed electric Semi is finally ready to scale.

The Semi factory opening is the latest big event Tesla has planned, following the unveiling of its production Cybercab robotaxi in Austin earlier this month. The company will next reveal the second-generation Roadster on Oct. 1.

The invite-only "Semi Rollout" event will likely include factory tours and rides in the truck. It's unclear whether Tesla will livestream it.

The 1.7 million-square-foot plant is designed to eventually build up to 50,000 Semis a year. The first truck came off its high-volume line in late April; it's most likely that the full ramp-up is still upcoming.

Tesla is quoting customers $290,000 for the 500-mile Long Range version, per Electrek . That's roughly 60% above the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017. The 325-mile Standard Range costs around $260,000, based on California incentive program data.

Tesla is betting fuel savings make up the difference, and the timing helps. US diesel averaged $6.53 a gallon this week, up around 74% from a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration . EU diesel prices also hit a record in mid-September, per European Commission data , as conflict in the Middle East squeezes supply.

Tesla heads into the Semi event with a big win. On Tuesday, ZET SCALE, a new shippers' alliance whose founding members include Microsoft and PepsiCo, named Tesla the primary manufacturer for an order of 2,500 battery-electric Class 8 trucks, per Catalyst Mobility (formerly CALSTART), one of the two groups running the program.

The order would nearly double the entire US electric Class 8 fleet. Kenworth, Volvo, and RIDE were named secondary suppliers.

"ZET SCALE's goals are exciting because they take the operational cost advantage and predictability that electricity provides and amplify it at scale," Tesla Semi program director Dan Priestley said in a statement.

Attendees are also expected to get a revised breakdown of the Semi's cost of ownership compared with diesel on Thursday.

Priestley said in May that Tesla expects to build "many thousands" of Semis by the end of 2026. He told Transport Topics the ramp would follow "a bit of an S-curve."

Tesla is also taking the Semi overseas. At the IAA Transportation show in Hannover, Germany, on Sept. 15, Tesla showed a European-spec Semi with up to 550 km (around 340 miles) of range when fully loaded. Customer deliveries are targeted for late 2027, per the trucking industry website Transport Topics .

articles.title: ‘Makes very little economic sense’: Ex-Trump energy secretary warns Trump against diesel export ban
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says he wants to ban America’s diesel exports, but his former energy secretary tells CNN this is a “bad idea” that will backfire.
articles.body: President Donald Trump says he wants to ban America’s diesel exports, but his former energy secretary tells CNN this is a “bad idea” that will backfire. “It’s one of those ideas that sounds good on the surface, but when you dig into it, it makes very little economic sense,” said Dan Brouillette, who served in Trump’s Cabinet from 2019 to 2021. Trump has faced intensifying calls from within his own party to do something to slash sky-high prices for diesel, the workhorse fuel that powers trains, trucks, tractors and construction vehicles. Echoing what experts have told CNN, Trump’s former energy secretary warned that choking off US diesel exports will encourage refiners to pull back on how much oil they process into gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. “Diesel comes from the same barrel of oil that gasoline does. So when you shut down diesel refining, you also shut down gasoline refining, which constrains the market, potentially raising the price of gasoline as well as diesel,” said Brouillette, now a distinguished visiting fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy. Even Trump’s current energy secretary, Chris Wright, is pouring cold water on the proposal. “The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” Wright said at an event in New York on Wednesday, according to Reuters. In other words, a diesel export ban could exacerbate what is already on track to be the biggest annual percentage increase for diesel prices on record. ‘It’s a bad idea’ In the short run, researchers say blocking the 1.5 million barrels of diesel that leave the United States daily could cause diesel prices to tumble – especially along the Gulf Coast and the Midwest, where many US refineries are located. But that excess diesel would likely be trapped in those areas because, as Brouillette notes, the United States does not have enough pipelines to transport the fuel to the East Coast and West Coast. “It’s a bad idea. It’s not something you want to impose,” Brouillette said of the proposed export ban. In the longer run, a US export ban risks incurring a chilling effect on foreign investment, he said. This would undermine the Trump administration’s goal of ramping up US refining capacity by expanding existing refineries, or even building the first major new refinery since 1977. “You’re sending a really poor investment signal to those who would invest in the United States to develop this infrastructure,” Brouillette said. “If they can’t count on you to be there, they’re not going to invest their money here.” Instead of banning US energy from getting sold overseas, Brouillette said the Trump administration should focus on building out energy infrastructure and oil production. This would mean providing tax and environmental incentives as well as ending the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war. Trump: ‘Let’s not send out the diesel’ A White House official told CNN on Monday that the Trump administration was not considering an export ban or even export restrictions, pointing to comments from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. But on Tuesday, Trump sang a very different tune: He indicated he’s pushed internally for a ban on US diesel exports, when asked about GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley and others calling for such a move. “I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel,’” Trump told reporters. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed the administration is “examining” whether a full or partial export ban is “feasible.” Big Oil doesn’t hold back The oil industry, which typically supports the Trump administration, has blasted the talk of an export ban. “We understand the administration is looking at every option to deliver relief, but restricting US energy exports would only compound the problem — exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers,” Mike Sommers, the president and CEO of the trade association American Petroleum Institute, said in a statement Tuesday. Brouillette said that if he were still in the Trump administration he would try to talk the president out of an export ban. “I would argue against the proposal, as I think many have inside of the White House,” he said. “But look, the ultimate decision maker is the president of the United States. The Cabinet is not elected. The president is, and he’s elected by the American people to make these decisions and it’s his right to make them.”

articles.title: Provident Fund wage ceiling rises to Rs 25,000: What does this mean for you? Top FAQs answered
articles.summary: The government’s decision to increase the provident fund wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000 is one of the most significant social security reforms
articles.body: The government’s decision to increase the provident fund wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000 is one of the most significant social security reforms in recent years. The move is expected to expand provident fund, pension and insurance coverage to additional employees, while also enhancing retirement benefits for many existing members.For employees, however, the immediate reaction may be simple: What does this mean for me?The answer depends on an employee’s wage structure, provident fund membership status and pension coverage. While some employees may see higher PF deductions, others may gain access to social security benefits for the first time. The change could also have a meaningful impact on long-term retirement savings and pension entitlement.Here are some key questions relevant for employees:Am I mandatorily required to be covered under PF?An employee whose statutory “wages” are up to Rs 25,000 will now fall within mandatory PF coverage. The biggest impact is likely to be on employees earning statutory wages above Rs 15,000 but up to Rs 25,000 who were previously outside mandatory coverage.It is important to note that the reference is to “wages” as defined under the Code on Social Security, 2020.How much could my PF contribution increase? Will my take-home salary reduce?For some employees, yes.The change is likely to affect two categories of employees:Employees whose monthly wages are Rs 25,000 or more, but whose PF contributions were restricted to the earlier statutory ceiling of Rs 15,000; andEmployees whose monthly wages are above Rs 15,000 and up to Rs 25,000, including those who are newly brought within mandatory PF coverage.For these employees, PF contributions will now be calculated on the revised ceiling of Rs 25,000 or on their actual ‘wages’, where these are below the revised ceiling.Employees already contributing on wages above Rs 25,000 will not see an increase in their total monthly PF contributions. However, the internal allocation of the employer’s contribution between provident fund and pension may still change.The impact will therefore depend on the employee’s wage level and the contribution basis followed before the change.Earlier, when PF contributions were restricted to the Rs 15,000 ceiling, the maximum monthly contribution was Rs 1,800. Following the increase in the ceiling to Rs 25,000, the monthly contribution can rise to Rs 3,000. Employees may therefore see an additional PF deduction of up to Rs 1,200 per month, reducing their monthly take-home salary.The impact may be more significant for an employee who was previously outside PF coverage but is now mandatorily covered. Since there was no corresponding deduction earlier, the employee’s take-home pay could reduce by the full amount of the new contribution.The reduction in take-home pay does not mean that the amount is lost or paid as a tax. It is deposited into the employee’s PF account and becomes part of the employee’s retirement savings. Employees will therefore have lower disposable income today, but a larger amount set aside for their long-term financial security.Does the change affect only PF or any other benefits also?No. The revised ceiling affects three important social security benefits:Employees’ Provident Fund, which helps employees build retirement savingsEmployees’ Pension Scheme, which provides a monthly pension to eligible membersEmployees’ Deposit-Linked Insurance Scheme, which provides employment-linked insurance protectionThe reform is therefore broader than a simple increase in PF deductions. It can affect an employee’s retirement savings, pension coverage / entitlement and insurance protection.Am I now mandatorily required to become a pension member?The increase in the ceiling means that employees earning statutory wages above Rs 15,000 but up to Rs 25,000 will now come within pension coverage, if such employees were not members under the Pension Scheme earlier.If I am an existing member of Pension Scheme, will there be any impact on my pension contributions?Yes.The employer’s contribution of 12% is divided between Provident Fund and Pension Scheme. The amount allocated to Pension Scheme is 8.33% of ‘wages’, subject to the applicable wage ceiling. The balance of the employer’s contribution is allocated to the employee’s Provident Fund account.With the ceiling increasing from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, the maximum monthly amount allocated to Pension Scheme can increase from Rs 1,250 to Rs 2,083. As a result, a larger portion of the employer’s contribution may be directed towards pension and a correspondingly smaller portion towards the employee’s Provident Fund account.This change can also affect existing pension members whose wages exceed Rs 25,000.Could my future pension entitlement increase?Potentially, yes.Monthly pension under Pension Scheme is linked to pensionable ‘wages’ (subject to the ceiling) and the employee’s pensionable service. Since the pensionable wage ceiling has increased from Rs 15,000 to Rs 25,000, eligible employees may receive a higher monthly pension upon retirement as compared with the amount calculated using the earlier ceiling.However, the increase will not be identical for every employee. The actual pension will depend on factors such as average pensionable wages, years of pensionable service, the period for which contributions are made at the revised ceiling and the applicable scheme conditions.What should I check on my salary slip / provident fund passbook to understand the impact?Employees may check the following aspects basis their salary slips / PF passbooks to understand the impact of the change:PF and Pension membership statusEmployee’s PF deduction;Employer’s total contribution;Wages used for calculating contributions;Allocation between EPF and EPS, where applicableLooking beyond the monthly deductionThe immediate focus for many employees will understandably be the potential reduction in take-home pay. However, the revised ceiling should also be viewed from a longer-term perspective.For employees newly brought within mandatory coverage, the change provides access to formal retirement savings, pension protection and employment-linked insurance coverage. For existing members, it may result in higher contributions, a different allocation between PF and pension, and a potentially higher pension benefit over time.Employees should therefore understand not only how much is being deducted from their salary, but also where the contribution is being deposited and how it supports their long-term financial security. PF savings can also provide financial support during important life events. Employees may make partial withdrawals for specified purposes, such as marriage, purchasing a house or medical treatment, through a simplified claims process on the EPFO online portal.The reform may therefore be viewed not merely as a higher monthly deduction, but as an investment in greater financial security for employees and their families.(The author, Puneet Gupta is Partner, People Advisory Services Tax at EY India. Viraj Lele, Director, EY India also contributed to the article)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Questions abound about how US-China 'notification mechanism' on AI will work as summit gets underway
articles.summary: Following a weekend of meetings with Chinese officials, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the idea of an AI "notification mechanism" that could lead...
articles.body:
Following a weekend of meetings with Chinese officials, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the idea of an AI "notification mechanism" that could lead to a shared vision of the technology between the largest economies in the world.

But since Sunday's announcement, questions have emerged about what this new mechanism would mean in practice — if it even comes to pass — as China has been silent on embracing the idea.

"Neither side trusts each other, and so they're making these sort of general symbolic promises that look good but have no details behind them," James Lewis of the Tech Policy Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday.

He added that any increased communication is a good thing, but every indication is that this will fall short of a "hotline" that serves as a direct connection between the two governments.

Instead, he said, the proposal "sounds pretty informal and I don't think that there's a desire right now to go beyond that."

Yet this effort at increased communication has emerged as the most likely area of agreement on artificial intelligence in the summit, which continues through Friday and will also feature talks on trade, the war in Iran, and many other issues.

Both the US and China have shown little interest in more wide-ranging moves on AI, such as regulating frontier models. It was a position that President Trump underlined Thursday morning when he posted that he wants to leave the overall sector "exactly where it is [and] that is China's position also."

Trump formally welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US on Wednesday evening with an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

The ceremony, according to the White House, featured a 100 foot-long red carpet, the United States Air Force Band, and a flyover from two B1 flyovers, among other touches.

A report in Politico on Tuesday described the notification system as little more than an informal plan to stay in touch, after Bessent described it slightly differently in an appearance on CNBC, calling it a "line so that we have constant communications, especially in the event of some kind of an incident."
